RICE.title: RICE Prioritisation
RICE.subtitle: Score = (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort  —  the higher the score, the sooner you build it
RICE.description: WHEN TO USE: comparing a backlog of features/ideas objectively. Reach = how many users this affects per period. Impact = per-user effect (3=massive, 2=high, 1=medium, 0.5=low, 0.25=minimal). Confidence = how sure you are (100/80/50%). Effort = person-months of work.

Read it: build top-ranked first. If two scores are close, the one with lower Effort de-risks faster. Beware inflated Reach — anchor it to real analytics, not hopes.

Weighted Scoring.title: Weighted Scoring Model
Weighted Scoring.subtitle: Rank options against criteria that matter differently — weights must sum to 100%
Weighted Scoring.description: WHEN TO USE: choosing between a few strategic options (e.g. which market to enter) where several criteria matter unequally. Set weights on row 8 (they auto-check to 100%). Score each option 1–5 on each criterion. Total = weighted sum.

Read it: highest total wins. Weights are where the debate should happen — get stakeholders to agree on weights BEFORE scoring, so the numbers aren't reverse-engineered to a favourite.

Value vs Effort.title: Value vs Effort (2×2)
Value vs Effort.subtitle: Quick Wins (high value, low effort) first; avoid the Money Pits
Value vs Effort.description: WHEN TO USE: a fast, visual triage. Rate Value and Effort 1–10. The scatter plots each item; the quadrant label is auto-assigned. Aim for the top-left: high value, low effort.

Read it: Quick Wins build momentum and trust. Big Bets need a strategic reason. Money Pits (low value, high effort) are usually a 'no'. Fill-ins are for spare capacity only.

Kano Model.title: Kano Model
Kano Model.subtitle: Classify features by how they drive satisfaction: Delighters, Performance, Must-be, Indifferent
Kano Model.description: WHEN TO USE: deciding what actually moves customer satisfaction. From paired survey questions, tally how many users put each feature in each category. Better = (Attractive+Performance)/total; Worse = −(Performance+Must-be)/total. The classification picks the most common vote.

Read it: top-left = Must-be (fix or lose trust), top-right = Performance (more is better), high Better + low Worse = Delighters (differentiators). Indifferent = don't over-invest.

WSJF.title: WSJF — Weighted Shortest Job First
WSJF.subtitle: SAFe prioritisation: WSJF = Cost of Delay ÷ Job Size. Do the highest WSJF first.
WSJF.description: WHEN TO USE: agile/SAFe backlogs where sequencing matters. Cost of Delay = User-Business Value + Time Criticality + Risk-reduction/Opportunity. Score each 1–10 (relative, not absolute). Job Size = relative effort. Short, high-value jobs rise to the top.

Read it: WSJF rewards small jobs that deliver value now. If everything is 'urgent', your Time Criticality scores aren't calibrated — force a spread from 1 to 10.

MoSCoW.title: MoSCoW
MoSCoW.subtitle: Scope a release: Must-have, Should-have, Could-have, Won't-have (this time)
MoSCoW.description: WHEN TO USE: agreeing scope for a release or MVP. Tag each item M/S/C/W. Rule of thumb: Must-haves should be ≤60% of effort, leaving slack for the unknown. The summary and pie update automatically.

Opportunity Scoring.title: Opportunity Scoring (Ulwick / ODI)
Opportunity Scoring.subtitle: Find under-served needs: Opportunity = Importance + max(Importance − Satisfaction, 0)
Opportunity Scoring.description: WHEN TO USE: outcome-driven innovation. Survey users on how IMPORTANT an outcome is and how SATISFIED they are today (both 1–10). High importance + low satisfaction = the biggest opportunity. Score >10 is a strong signal, >15 is exceptional.

WHEN TO USE: outcome-driven innovation. Survey users on how IMPORTANT an outcome is and how SATISFIED they are today (both 1–10). High importance + low satisfaction = the biggest opportunity. Score >10 is a strong signal, >15 is exceptional.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)

Read it: attack the highest opportunity scores — that's where users care a lot and current solutions disappoint. Well-served outcomes (high importance, high satisfaction) are table-stakes, not differentiators.

BCG Matrix.title: BCG Growth–Share Matrix
BCG Matrix.subtitle: Portfolio view: Stars, Cash Cows, Question Marks, Dogs — decide where to invest, milk, or exit
BCG Matrix.description: WHEN TO USE: allocating money/attention across a portfolio of products or lines. Market Growth = the market's annual growth (invest if high). Relative Market Share = your share ÷ largest rival's share (>1 means you lead). Bubble size = revenue. Category is auto-assigned at the 10% / 1.0x lines.

Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)

Play: fund Stars, milk Cash Cows to fund Stars/Question Marks, pick 1–2 Question Marks to back hard, and divest Dogs. Everything can't be a Star — a healthy portfolio needs Cash Cows paying the bills.

Ansoff Matrix.title: Ansoff Growth Matrix
Ansoff Matrix.subtitle: Four growth vectors, rising risk: Market Penetration → Product Development / Market Development → Diversification
Ansoff Matrix.description: WHEN TO USE: choosing HOW to grow. Existing product + existing market = Penetration (lowest risk). New product OR new market = medium risk. New product AND new market = Diversification (highest risk). Enter expected revenue and a success probability; risk-adjusted value ranks them.
raw_rows: Four growth vectors, rising risk: Market Penetration → Product Development / Market Development → Diversification

WHEN TO USE: choosing HOW to grow. Existing product + existing market = Penetration (lowest risk). New product OR new market = medium risk. New product AND new market = Diversification (highest risk). Enter expected revenue and a success probability; risk-adjusted value ranks them.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)

Read it: growth gets riskier as you move away from what you know. Weight your roadmap toward penetration for cash, a measured bet or two on adjacent products/markets, and diversify only with strong conviction and a ring-fenced budget.

Porter 5 Forces.title: Porter's Five Forces
Porter 5 Forces.subtitle: How attractive is this market? Score each force 1 (benign) to 5 (brutal). Lower total = more attractive.
Porter 5 Forces.description: WHEN TO USE: assessing structural profitability of a market before entering or doubling down. Score the THREAT level of each force. The radar shows your risk shape; overall attractiveness = 6 − average score (higher is better).

Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)
High capital + network effects deter, but funding is available
Large chains negotiate hard on commission
Home cooking, dine-in, direct restaurant apps
Read it: a market where four forces are '5' can still be entered — but only with a wedge (a segment rivals ignore) and a durable moat. Use this to choose WHERE to compete, not just whether.

North Star.title: North Star Metric
North Star.subtitle: One metric that captures the value users get — decomposed into the inputs a team can actually move
North Star.description: WHEN TO USE: aligning the whole team behind value, not vanity. Pick an NSM that rises only when customers succeed (e.g. 'weekly orders delivered on time'). Decompose it into 2–4 input metrics you can influence. Track actual vs target monthly.

1 · North Star decomposition   (NSM = Active users × Orders per user × On-time rate)

Read it: if input drivers are all green but the NSM lags, your model of value is wrong — revisit which inputs truly cause the outcome. A good NSM is a leading indicator of revenue, not revenue itself.

AARRR Funnel.title: AARRR — Pirate Metrics
AARRR Funnel.subtitle: The lifecycle funnel: Acquisition → Activation → Retention → Revenue → Referral. Find the leakiest step.
AARRR Funnel.description: WHEN TO USE: diagnosing where users drop off. Enter the count reaching each stage. Step conversion = this stage ÷ previous stage. % of top = this stage ÷ acquisition. The biggest drop is usually your highest-leverage fix.
raw_rows: The lifecycle funnel: Acquisition → Activation → Retention → Revenue → Referral. Find the leakiest step.

Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)
Read it: don't pour money into Acquisition if Activation is leaking. Fix the funnel bottom-up — retention first, because retained users make every other number cheaper.

HEART.title: Google HEART Framework
HEART.subtitle: Measure UX quality across Happiness, Engagement, Adoption, Retention, Task success
HEART.description: WHEN TO USE: turning fuzzy 'good experience' into trackable metrics. For each category pick ONE signal metric, set current & target. % attainment shows how close you are. Don't track all five if only two matter for this feature.

Read it: pair each metric with a Goal→Signal→Metric logic so you're measuring the behaviour that proves the goal, not the easiest number to collect. Retention and Task success are usually the truthful ones.

Unit Economics.title: Unit Economics — LTV, CAC & Payback
Unit Economics.subtitle: Does each customer make more than they cost? The single most important growth question.
Unit Economics.description: WHEN TO USE: validating that growth is profitable, not just fast. Enter the four blue inputs. Lifetime = 1 ÷ monthly churn. LTV = ARPU × gross margin × lifetime. Aim for LTV:CAC ≥ 3 and payback ≤ 12 months.
raw_rows: Does each customer make more than they cost? The single most important growth question.

WHEN TO USE: validating that growth is profitable, not just fast. Enter the four blue inputs. Lifetime = 1 ÷ monthly churn. LTV = ARPU × gross margin × lifetime. Aim for LTV:CAC ≥ 3 and payback ≤ 12 months.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)
CAC — cost to acquire a customer
Read it: churn is the silent killer — halving churn doubles lifetime and LTV. If LTV:CAC < 3, either lower CAC (better targeting/organic), raise ARPU, or cut churn before you scale spend.

Cohort Retention.title: Cohort Retention
Cohort Retention.subtitle: Track how each monthly signup group sticks around over time — the truest measure of product value
Cohort Retention.description: WHEN TO USE: judging real stickiness and product-market fit. Enter cohort size (Month 0 users) and how many are still active each later month. Retention % is auto-calculated. A flattening curve (retention stops falling) is the signal of PMF.
raw_rows: Track how each monthly signup group sticks around over time — the truest measure of product value

WHEN TO USE: judging real stickiness and product-market fit. Enter cohort size (Month 0 users) and how many are still active each later month. Retention % is auto-calculated. A flattening curve (retention stops falling) is the signal of PMF.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)
Read it: if every cohort keeps declining to near-zero, you don't have PMF yet. A curve that flattens at, say, 28% means a loyal core — newer cohorts flattening HIGHER means your product is improving.

PMF Survey.title: Product-Market Fit Survey (Sean Ellis test)
PMF Survey.subtitle: Ask users: 'How would you feel if you could no longer use this product?' ≥40% 'very disappointed' = PMF signal
PMF Survey.description: WHEN TO USE: gauging whether you have product-market fit. Survey engaged users. Count responses in each bucket. The score = 'very disappointed' ÷ (all answers except N/A). 40% is the benchmark from thousands of startups.

WHEN TO USE: gauging whether you have product-market fit. Survey engaged users. Count responses in each bucket. The score = 'very disappointed' ÷ (all answers except N/A). 40% is the benchmark from thousands of startups.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)
N/A – I no longer use it

Read it: below 40%, segment the 'very disappointed' users — who are they, what do they love? Double down on that persona and use-case before broadening. This survey guides positioning as much as product.

A-B Test.title: A/B Test Significance Calculator
A-B Test.subtitle: Is the difference real or noise? Two-proportion z-test with 95% / 99% thresholds
A-B Test.description: WHEN TO USE: deciding if a variant genuinely beats control. Enter visitors and conversions for each. The calculator returns conversion rates, relative uplift, a z-score and whether it clears the 95% (z>1.96) and 99% (z>2.576) bars. Aim for a pre-set sample size, don't peek early.

WHEN TO USE: deciding if a variant genuinely beats control. Enter visitors and conversions for each. The calculator returns conversion rates, relative uplift, a z-score and whether it clears the 95% (z>1.96) and 99% (z>2.576) bars. Aim for a pre-set sample size, don't peek early.
Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)

Read it: 'not significant' doesn't mean 'no effect' — it may mean too little data. Decide your sample size and duration up front. Practical significance (is the uplift worth shipping?) matters as much as statistical significance.

OKR Tracker.title: OKR Tracker
OKR Tracker.subtitle: Objectives are the ambition; Key Results are the measurable proof. Track progress, not activity.
OKR Tracker.description: WHEN TO USE: quarterly goal-setting and mid-cycle check-ins. Each Objective gets 2–4 Key Results with a Start, Current and Target. Progress = (Current − Start) ÷ (Target − Start). 0.7 is often 'success' for a stretch KR — 1.0 everywhere means you set them too easy.

Legend:  Yellow = your inputs (edit these)    ·    White = live formulas (leave alone)

Read it: OKRs measure outcomes, not tasks. 'Ship feature X' is not a Key Result; 'raise retention to 40%' is. Review weekly, grade at quarter-end, and don't tie 100%-or-bust bonuses to stretch OKRs — it kills ambition.
